newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra to squeeze defence money from bureaucrats.
newsitem.headline: Canberra to squeeze defence money from bureaucrats.

text.p: The Australian government announced a sweeping programme for defence efficiency on Friday, with the aim of shifting 10 percent of the defence budget away from bureaucratic support services and into weapons and training.
"We're going to shift expenditure from the bureaucracy of defence into the front-line of defence," Prime Minister John Howard said on television.
"There'll be more money to spend on equipment and on the sharp end, the front end," he said. "So it's fewer bureaucrats and more soldiers."

Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said about 8,000 support jobs would go. Many of them would be uniformed staff working in the defence bureaucracy, but half of the redundant service personnel would be moved into combat positions, he said.
At present, about A$6 billion of the A$10 billion defence budget actually goes to the Navy, Army and Air Force, the remainder being spent on administration and the like.
McLachlan said the reform programme would begin by selling off surplus property to raise A$500 million.
But the biggest impact would be in recurrent savings.
"At maturity there will be at least A$770 million with the possibility of A$1 billion annual costs cut from support areas and redirected into enhancing military capabilities," he said.
McLachlan said money had to be squeezed from the inefficient bureaucracy because, while Australia's defence spending was tending to fall, the end of the Cold War had stoked instability.
"Post Cold War, things are less certain than they were," he said, noting that defence spending had fallen from 2.6 percent of gross domestic product 10 years ago to 1.8 percent now.
Australia's neighbours were also getting stronger, said Malcolm McIntosh, the former British defence procurement chief who prepared the Australian reform strategy.
"Not that long ago, we were a mini-superpower in our own region," he told reporters.
"Our economy was substantially larger and the amount we bought for our defence dollar was substantially larger than anyone else around our region."

"That's changing and changing very quickly, if for no other reason at all but that the economies around region are growing rapidly and all of those countries are now in a position to acquire the sort of things that only we could afford a few years ago."
McLachlan listed some of items he needed to find money for:
-- Airborne-early-warning radar aircraft.
-- Better weapons and sensors on warships.
-- More helicopter and ground transport for the army.
-- Modernising the F/A-18 Hornet fighters and F-111 strike bombers.
"And I could add 40 more to that list, he said.
"In the near future that money is not readily available so we've got to do it in other ways."
Australia's neighbours do increasingly operate the sort of equipment on which it once had a regional monopoly.
For example, Australia alone in the region operated leading-edge fighter aircraft from World War Two until the 1980s.

Even now its 70-odd Hornets are a thoroughly up-to-date fighter force -- but Malaysia operates Hornets, too, and Indonesia has a handful of the slightly smaller but quite modern F-16. -- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
